idea: Halftone of an 1870s studio portrait of Frederick Douglass, stern and direct, with his line from the 1845 Narrative below: 'I understood the pathway from slavery to freedom.' He meant learning to read, which he did in secret. It's a powerful case for literacy with a great face on it.

Halftone of Mary Garrity's c. 1893 portrait of journalist Ida B. Wells, captioned 'A mob wrecked her newspaper office in 1892. She kept writing.' The Memphis Free Speech was destroyed after her editorial on lynching, and she carried on the work from the North. It's for journalists and anyone who believes in printing the truth when it costs something.

Detroit Publishing Co. photograph of the Boston Public Library's McKim building, cropped tight on the words carved above its entrance: 'FREE TO ALL'. No caption needed. It's a handsome piece of architecture and a three-word argument for public libraries.

Gabriel Harrison's 1854 daguerreotype of young Walt Whitman, hat tilted and shirt open, captioned 'Leaves of Grass, 1855. Self-published. No name on the title page, just this picture.' An engraving of this image was the frontispiece of the first edition, which Whitman paid to print. It's for indie authors and zine-makers.

A. F. Bradley's 1907 photograph of Mark Twain in his white suit, captioned 'mark twain (n.): a leadsman's call, two fathoms. Safe water.' Mississippi riverboat crews used the call for a depth of 12 feet, and the former pilot Samuel Clemens took it as his pen name. A wordy shirt for people who like knowing where names come from.

Archive photograph looking down into the round Main Reading Room of the Library of Congress, captioned 'After the British burned it in 1814, Jefferson sold Congress 6,487 of his own books.' Congress paid $23,950 for them in 1815 to restart the library. It's a gorgeous room and a story about rebuilding with books.

Halftone of an 18th-century wooden hand press with an excerpt from the epitaph Benjamin Franklin wrote for himself at 22: 'The Body of B. Franklin, Printer; Like the Cover of an old Book, Its Contents torn out...' He called himself a printer before anything else. It's for printers and book people who like wit about mortality.

The 1888 photograph of young Helen Keller with her teacher Anne Sullivan, captioned 'w-a-t-e-r. April 5, 1887.' That was the day Sullivan spelled the word into Keller's hand at a water pump, and Keller first understood that things have names. It's a shirt about the moment language arrives.

US Army photograph of a GI reading a small, wide paperback in a foxhole, captioned 'Armed Services Edition. 123 million books shipped to the troops, 1943–47.' The program printed more than 1,300 titles and helped rescue The Great Gatsby from obscurity. It's for readers who think books are supplies, not luxuries.

Halftone of the front page of the Cherokee Phoenix (1828), set in English and in Sequoyah's syllabary, captioned 'Sequoyah could not read any language. So he made one readable.' He finished the syllabary in 1821, and Cherokee literacy spread within a few years. It's beautiful type with a story about invention.

An old photograph of the Chi Rho page of the Book of Kells (c. 800), its swirling knotwork filling the whole leaf, captioned 'Three letters. One page.' The page decorates just the first letters of Christ's name in Greek, XPI. It's the most beautiful case for taking your time.

Halftone of Marie Curie at her laboratory bench, captioned 'Her notebooks are still radioactive. Readers sign a waiver.' Her papers in the Bibliothèque nationale de France are kept in lead-lined boxes, and visitors wear protective gear. It's a shirt about books that are dangerous in the most literal way.

Archive photograph of Duke Humfrey's Library in Oxford's Bodleian, with its dark oak shelves and painted ceiling, with a line from the oath every reader still declares: 'not to bring into the Library, or kindle therein, any fire or flame.' It's dry, old-fashioned and still in force, for people who take libraries seriously.

An expedition photograph of Shackleton's snowbound hut at Cape Royds, captioned 'Aurora Australis, 1908. The first book printed in Antarctica.' It was printed in the hut during the Nimrod expedition and bound in boards from packing cases. It's for people who'd make a book anywhere.

Frederick Hollyer's 1887 portrait of William Morris, with his line: 'Have nothing in your houses that you do not know to be useful, or believe to be beautiful.' Morris founded the Kelmscott Press in 1891 and revived fine printing. It's a design manifesto from the man behind the Kelmscott Chaucer.

Carl Van Vechten's 1935 portrait of Gertrude Stein, captioned 'Rose is a rose is a rose is a rose.' The line comes from her 1913 poem 'Sacred Emily'. It's for people who like a sentence that keeps insisting until it means something new.

Napoleon Sarony's 1882 photograph of Oscar Wilde reclining in a velvet coat, captioned 'Burrow-Giles v. Sarony, 1884. The picture that made photographs copyrightable. Now it belongs to everyone.' The Supreme Court case over this image confirmed that photographs could be protected like writing. A clever shirt about authorship, with Wilde looking fabulous.

Archive photograph of grown men and women at school desks in rural Kentucky, captioned 'Moonlight Schools, 1911. Classes on bright nights so adults could find the road.' Cora Wilson Stewart expected about 150 learners on the first night, and around 1,200 came. It's a hopeful shirt about learning to read at any age.

US Fish and Wildlife Service portrait of Rachel Carson, captioned 'Silent Spring, 1962. One book. DDT banned in the US, 1972.' Her book started the modern environmental movement. It's for people who believe writing can change law.

Halftone portrait of Upton Sinclair, with his own line about The Jungle (1906): 'I aimed at the public's heart, and by accident I hit it in the stomach.' The book helped bring in the Pure Food and Drug Act and the Meat Inspection Act that same year. A funny, honest shirt about what books actually do.
